<reason>Both sides argued well, but PRO made the debate easier to decide. CON built a genuinely interesting case (tip as worker property vs. service charge as house revenue, DC/Maine server opposition, the Danny Meyer reversal) and landed real hits — especially that PRO's A1 "write it into law" imported a statute not in the motion, and that a tip-credit floor already exists. But CON conceded, speech by speech, that the menu should be legible, the floor should rise, and the kitchen should share; PRO's "CON has built the PRO world and objects to its name" tracked the motion's actual language ("rather than rely on customer guilt") and left CON defending only a voluntary gratuity on top of a living wage — something the motion does not clearly forbid. CON's textual "replace" argument in the closing was sharp but arrived after most of the ground was ceded. PRO also neutralized the "one boss" harassment counter (the boss already controls sections and hours) and turned CON's own tip-pooling remedy against the owner-discretion objection. CON never answered the race/gender variance point. PRO's dismissal of the DC/Maine servers was its weakest moment, and PRO suffered more clipping, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B4.5–B4.6 consolidation of CON's concessions ("the tip is no longer load-bearing... That is the motion"), following CON's A1.6/A2.4/A2.5 admissions, forced CON into a narrow textual fight over "replace" and left variance-on-the-worker as the only live disagreement.</best_rebuttal>
